battle.name: 李軌起事
battle.brief: 大業十三年（617）冬，蜀郡人李軌在益州起兵，旬月據成都、逼郡縣，隋廷遠在江都，鞭長莫及。起義軍以削尖竹木、舊銅器改製的長矛為骨幹兵器，李軌自稱王，與官軍在成都平原、劍門道對峙數月而平。卡面所示的古埃及長矛，正是這班鄉民唯一做得起的矛形原版：銅頭綁木杆，換成削尖竹桿與敲平舊銅。

kit.name: 埃及長矛
kit.history: 早王朝時期的長矛，銅或青銅矛頭綁在木杆上。埃及人用它守城垣，後來也用它收復失地。

countries: 李軌起事是隋大業十三年（617）冬在益州爆發的一場地方叛亂，戰線主要落在益州治所成都（隋稱成都郡，唐復稱蜀郡）與周邊郡縣。叛方是一個以成都為核心、靠鄉里關係拼湊起來的起義集團，首領李軌是蜀人，在隋朝先後做過地方縣尉與中央部曹之官，熟悉郡縣的戶籍、倉場與驛傳，因此對「一郡之內有多少糧、多少人、多少兵」一清二楚。他身邊的核心是成都平原的鄉豪、渠帥與熟悉官署內情的前隋吏員，外圍則是盆周山地與邊地的部眾、逃戶逃兵，以及被攤派未還的役夫。史稱其聚眾數萬，但能列為骨幹、持械作戰者只佔少數，編制上沒有常備建制，全靠臨時推舉的將帥與部曲分統，事權極易分裂。官方一方是隋朝在益州的州郡官府：益州刺史與成都郡的太守、郡丞以下仍各據城邑，倚靠州郡兵、縣兵與徵發的鄉兵固守城牆與渡口，援軍則指望自漢中沿劍門道東進，或溯長江而上。隋廷本人在江都，鞭長莫及，只能靠詔書與零星派出的部隊維持秩序。李軌起事之後不到一年，唐取代隋，益州歸入唐朝，鎮壓與接管的工作改由唐朝的益州大都督府接手。
countriesEn: Li Gui's Revolt was a local rebellion that broke out in Yizhou in the winter of Daye 13 (617 CE), with the front running mainly through the provincial seat of Chengdu (called Chengdu Commandery under the Sui, restored to the name Shu Commandery under the Tang) and the commanderies and counties around it. The rebel side was an improvised coalition put together around the city out of village connections. Its leader, Li Gui, was a native of Shu who had served the Sui first as a county commandant and later as a ministry official in the capital, and who therefore knew the household registers, the granaries and the courier stations of the commanderies intimately, so that he knew exactly how much grain, how many people and how many troops each commandery contained. His inner core was made up of the wealthy villagers, local militia leaders (qu shuai) and former Sui functionaries of the Chengdu plain who knew the inside of the official offices; around them stood the mountain and frontier populations of the basin rim, runaway households, deserters and levies conscripted and never sent home. The histories say the muster numbered tens of thousands, but only a small part of these could be formed up and fight with weapons, and there was no standing establishment at all: command fell to self-appointed generals and locally raised bands, and authority could easily split. The official side was the Sui administration of Yizhou: the provincial governor and the prefect, deputy prefect and county magistrates of Chengdu Commandery each still held a city, and relied on provincial, commandery and county troops together with conscripted village levies to hold the walls and the ferry crossings. Relief could only come from Hanzhong along the Jiange road or by ascending the Yangtze. The Sui court sat at Jiangdu, far too distant to impose order, and could keep a grip only through edicts and the occasional detachment. Less than a year after the rising the Tang replaced the Sui in Yizhou, and the work of suppression and takeover passed to the Tang commandery administration of Yizhou.
people: 李軌是這場起事唯一在通行史籍中留下姓名的首領。蜀人出身，早年仕隋，先為地方縣尉，後入京任部曹官員，一說為倉部郎中，掌與度支、糧運相關的事務——這正好解釋了他為何熟悉各郡縣的倉場與轉運。大業末年局勢崩壞，他辭官返蜀，於大業十三年冬在成都聚眾起事，自稱王，旬月之間取得成都周邊郡縣的響應。與他同處成都的，還有被囚於此的隋室宗室蜀王楊秀。楊秀是隋文帝楊堅的兒子，與煬帝楊廣同母，太原起兵後被挾持在江都，後隨宇文化及之眾北走而死。起義發生的時候，蜀郡城內同時存在「囚禁的宗室」與「失控的吏員」兩種政治資源，這是理解李軌起事背景時不能略過的細節。李淵於同年五月在長安起兵，翌年正月建立唐朝；宇文化及在次年三月於江都弒隋煬帝，隨即率眾北還，成都一帶的權力真空正是在這個時段形成。唐廷平定蜀中後，派韋仁壽出任益州大都督府長史，接掌蜀地軍政；一說起義軍的殘部正是由這支部隊在成都平原擊潰。至於起事集團其他首領的名號，通行史籍記載極為零碎，多以「渠帥」「部曲首」概之，後世記載亦互有出入，因此不宜逐一指認。
peopleEn: Li Gui is the only leader of this rising whose name survives in the standard historical records. A native of Shu, he entered Sui service early, first as a county commandant and later as a ministry official in the capital, in one account as a bureau director in the Ministry of Works in charge of finance and the transport of grain; this is precisely why he knew the granaries and the transport circuits of the commanderies so well. As the Sui order collapsed at the end of Daye, he left office and returned to Shu, mustered followers at Chengdu in the winter of Daye 13 and proclaimed himself king, and within ten days drew the response of the commanderies and counties around Chengdu. In the same city stood Yang Xiu, prince of Shu, a member of the Sui imperial clan who was held prisoner there. Yang Xiu was a son of Emperor Wen of Sui, Yang Jian, and a half-brother of Yang Guang, the Jian emperor; after the rising at Taiyuan he was carried off to Jiangdu and later died when Yuwen Huaji's men moved north with him. When the revolt broke out, two kinds of political resource existed side by side inside the walls of Shu: an imprisoned prince and functionaries who had ceased to answer to anyone. That detail cannot be skipped when one tries to understand the background of Li Gui's rising. Li Yuan raised troops at Chang'an in May of the same year and founded the Tang in the first month of the following year; Yuwen Huaji murdered the Jian emperor at Jiangdu in the third month of the year after that and led his men north, and the vacuum of authority in the Chengdu region was formed precisely in that stretch of time. After the rising was put down, the Tang court sent Wei Renshou to serve as chief administrator of the great commandery headquarters of Yizhou and to take over military and civil authority in Shu; in one account it was this column that broke the remnants of the insurgents on the Chengdu plain. As for the names of the other leaders in the rebel group, the standard records are extremely fragmentary, referring to them mostly as local militia leaders or band chiefs, and later compilations disagree with one another, so it is wiser not to identify them one by one.
kits: 卡面這件古埃及長矛，是古埃及早王朝的標準長矛：青銅矛頭以套口銜接木杆，再以繩纏或瀝青固定，柄尾留一截供握持與配重。它本身並沒有出現在隋末蜀中的戰場上，但它的形制恰好是起義軍唯一做得起的樣板——青銅矛頭加一根木杆，正是最原始也最平價的長矛做法；蜀中鄉民不必仿製什麼，只要把削尖的竹桿與木杆、敲平的舊銅器、破鍋片、犁頭纏上麻繩，就等於把這件遠古標本原樣復刻一次。史書沒有留下李軌部眾用何種矛的記載，這一點可以確定；但同一時段的隋末戰役已留下旁證：唐軍近身靠鐵矛與馬槊，地方郡兵與義軍則大量使用自製的長矛。相對之下，蜀中起義軍的矛更粗陋：尾端無鐏，柄身不均，多在近身纏鬥中發揮作用；上山的長柄矛另加鐵箍與護手，以便在狹窄的徑路上揮砸而不致折斷。官軍一方的步卒用隋制長矛，鐵矛頭安於長桿；槊則是更長更重的長柄兵器，供武官與重裝騎兵使用。與長矛同樣大量配發的還有方盾、角弓、臂甲、長刀，以及以竹木為主的號旗與鼓角；騎兵配馬槊與短兵器，弓弩則集中佈置於城防與隘口，用以射殺逼近的攻城者。攻城與守城的器材多取本地材料：撞竿、雲梯、攻城車、拒馬與鹿角、壕柵、雉堞，成都平原的竹木供應充足，製作週期卻短，一夜之間便可立起或拆去。糧秣方面，益州是隋的餘糧區之一，成都平原靠都江堰與各處渠堰灌溉，稻米與竹筍、獵獲可支應大軍；糧食轉運依賴岷江、沱江與長江三級水道，以及劍門道、褒斜道、金牛道幾條南北陸路，蜀道之險使遠道來援遲滯，也令起義軍得以據險而動。
kitsEn: The Egyptian spear on the card is the standard spear of the early dynastic period in ancient Egypt: a bronze head fitted onto a wooden shaft by a socket and lashed with cord or pitch, with a length of shaft left at the rear for gripping and balance. It never appeared on a battlefield in Shu in the late Sui period, but its configuration happens to be the one template the insurgents could actually afford: a bronze head on a wooden shaft is the oldest and cheapest way to make a spear, so the villagers of Shu did not have to imitate anything. They only had to take a sharpened bamboo or wooden shaft, flatten an old bronze vessel, a fragment of a broken cauldron or a ploughshare, bind the lot with hemp cord, and the effect was a faithful copy of that ancient original. What the histories do not record is which kind of spear Li Gui's followers carried, and that much can be stated with certainty; the campaigns of the same late Sui period supply the circumstantial evidence instead. Tang troops fought at close quarters with iron spears and long lances, while local commandery troops and insurgent bands relied on large numbers of self-made spears. The spears of the Shu insurgents were cruder still: no butt-spike, uneven shafts, weapons that did their work in the clinch of close fighting, while the long-handled spears carried into the hills were further strengthened with iron bands and hand-guards, so that they would survive being swung in narrow paths without snapping. The government infantry used regulation Sui spears with iron heads on long hafts, and the shuo, a longer and heavier pole weapon, went to officers and heavily armed cavalry. Distributed in large numbers alongside the spears were rectangular shields, horn bows, arm guards, long sabres, and flags and drums made mainly of bamboo and wood. Cavalry carried mounted lances and short weapons, while crossbows and bows were concentrated on city defences and at passes, to shoot down men who came up against the walls. Siege and defensive equipment was largely taken from local materials: battering poles, scaling ladders, siege cars, chevaux-de-frise and antler obstacles, trenches and stakes, and parapets. The Chengdu plain supplied bamboo and timber in abundance, yet the build cycle was short, so a battery could be raised or dismantled overnight. As for supply, Yizhou was one of the Sui's surplus-grain regions; the Chengdu plain was irrigated by the Dujiangyan works and by numerous canal and weir systems, and rice with bamboo shoots and game could provision an army. Grain moved on the three tiers of waterway - the Min, the Tuo and the Yangtze - and along several north-south land routes including the Jiange, Baoxie and Jinniu roads. The difficulty of the Shu roads made distant relief slow and hesitant, and it also let the insurgents move from one strong position to another.
tactics: 起義軍的戰法由形勢決定：李軌既無可與官軍野戰的兵員，也沒有攻城器械，因此採取的是先取近據、以險待援的辦法。起事當夜，靠熟悉城防的內應與鄉里武裝同時動手，控制成都城門、府庫與橋頭；得手後即分兵馳往周邊縣城，多半不攻而取，或以少量兵力圍逼迫令歸附，再向外郡傳播。兵眾既無編制，臨陣多以鄉里同族為單位，旌旗、鼓角與號令難以統一。在山地與丘陵地帶，起義軍採游擊與伏擊：熟悉獸道、堰渠、山徑與渡口，避開關隘大道，在官軍糧隊與驛使的必經之處設伏，斷其糧道；遇官軍大隊則退入塢堡、村寨或山林，以地形抵人數。這樣的戰術能拖住遠道而來的援軍，卻無法在平原上吃掉敵方主力。官軍一方的部署是典型的守點求援：以成都、雒縣、郫縣等城邑與渡口、倉場為核心，郡兵與縣兵固守城牆，倚角弓與弩壓制城外逼近之敵，以木柵、拒馬、壕溝遲滯對方；一有戰況便以驛騎傳報漢中與利州，請求西川以外的援兵。援軍只能沿劍門道魚貫而入，隊形被山道拉成長線，前後隊難以互相策應，這正是起義軍得以游擊的空間。唐朝接手後，鎮壓與整編並行：先以騎兵快速打散聚集的部眾，再收編降卒為州郡兵，恢復被毀的城垣、橋樑與倉場，重編戶籍，並沿主要驛道設置傳馬與警候，使消息由成都傳漢中只需數日。
tacticsEn: The method of the insurgents was dictated by their situation: with no troops fit to meet the government army in the open field and no siege equipment, they adopted the plan of seizing the nearest strongpoints first and holding the passes while waiting for relief. On the night the rising began, insiders who knew the city defences and the village bands acted together and took the gates of Chengdu, the treasury and the bridges. Once they held the city they split off columns to ride for the surrounding county seats; most were taken without a real assault, or were talked into submission by a small force parked outside, and from there word was carried to the outer commanderies. Since the multitude had no establishment, units in the line were grouped by village and clan, and banners, drums and orders could hardly be made uniform. In the hills and the broken country the insurgents used harassment and ambush: they knew the drove roads, the weir paths, the tracks and the fords, avoided the main passes, and lay in wait where the government's grain convoys and courier riders had to pass, cutting the supply line; when a government column appeared in strength they withdrew into fortified villages, stockades or wooded ravines, letting the ground stand in for numbers. Such tactics could hold up relief that came from far away, but they could not destroy an enemy main force in the open plain. The government deployment was the classic pattern of holding points and asking for help: with the cities of Chengdu, Luoxian and Pixian, together with the ferries and the granaries, as the core, commandery and county troops manned the walls, bows and crossbows kept attackers outside the walls under fire, and wooden fences, chevaux-de-frise and ditches slowed the assault. The first report of any fighting was carried by relay horse to Hanzhong and Lizhou, asking for troops from beyond western Shu. Such reinforcements could only file in single file along the Jiange road, the column stretched into a long thread by the mountain track, so that rear and leading elements could not support one another, and that was the space in which the insurgents operated. Once the Tang took over, suppression and reorganization went hand in hand: cavalry first broke up the gathered bands, surrendered men were enrolled as provincial and commandery troops, damaged walls, bridges and granaries were restored, the registers were rewritten, and relay horses and watch posts were set along the main post roads, so that news now travelled from Chengdu to Hanzhong in a matter of days.
data: 關於這場起事，可核對的數字極為稀少，以下只列可以確定的部分。時間上，起事在隋大業十三年（617）冬，通常繫於十一月，其後數月內平定，跨度不過數月，遠短於同期竇建德、李密兩部長年的拉鋸。地域上，戰場是益州治所成都（隋稱成都郡，唐復稱蜀郡）及其外圍；益州是隋朝領郡最多的州之一，領郡十餘，成都郡居首。地理尺度上，成都至漢中陸路約六百里山路，至長安經劍門道約一千五百里；隋廷所在的江都距成都更遠，陸路逾二千里，水路須溯長江穿過三峽，順流數旬、逆流更久，調兵與轉糧極為遲緩。兵眾方面，史稱李軌「聚眾數萬」，但這是當時的概數，包含了隨之響應的鄉里人戶，實際列陣可戰者遠少於此；官軍方面，益州州郡兵與縣兵分散各城，總數無從考訂，外來援軍亦無確數。糧食方面，益州是隋廷倚重的餘糧與轉運之區，成都平原的渠堰灌田面積廣，稻米年成可支大軍數月之食，這是起義軍能據蜀自立、官軍也能就地取糧的共同前提。此外，隋自612年起三次征伐高句麗，兵役與轉輸未停，全國戶口銳減的背景下，各地「起兵而據郡」的風氣在617年前後密集出現，益州即是其中之一。
dataEn: Very few verifiable figures survive for this rising, and only those that can be stated with confidence are given here. In time, the revolt fell in the winter of Daye 13 (617), usually dated to the eleventh month, and was put down within the following few months, a span of no more than a few months and far shorter than the years-long struggle between the forces of Dou Jiande and Li Mi in the same period. In place, the battlefield was the provincial seat of Chengdu (Chengdu Commandery under the Sui, Shu Commandery again under the Tang) and its surroundings; Yizhou was among the Sui provinces with the most commanderies, a dozen or more, with Chengdu Commandery at their head. In terms of distance, the road from Chengdu to Hanzhong runs about six hundred li of mountain track, and the road to Chang'an through the Jiange pass about fifteen hundred li; Jiangdu, where the Sui court sat, lay much further, more than two thousand li by land, and by water it meant ascending the Yangtze through the Three Gorges, a matter of weeks downstream and longer still against the current, so that moving troops and grain was extremely slow. On the size of the forces, the histories say Li Gui 'mustered tens of thousands', but that is a rough contemporary figure which includes the village households that answered the call; the number who could actually be formed up and fight was far smaller. On the government side, the provincial, commandery and county troops of Yizhou were dispersed among separate cities, their total cannot be checked, and the number of outside reinforcements is likewise unrecorded. As for supply, Yizhou was one of the regions on which the Sui court relied for surplus grain and transport, and the irrigated area of the Chengdu plain was wide, so that a good rice harvest could feed an army for months - the shared premise that allowed the insurgents to stand on Shu territory and also allowed the government troops to draw grain on the spot. Finally, from 612 the Sui had waged three campaigns against Goguryeo without halting the levies and the transport, and against a background of a national population sharply reduced, risings that took a commandery and held it appeared thickly in various places around 617, and Yizhou was one of them.
cause: 大業十三年（617）冬的李軌起事，根源在隋朝國家機器的整體崩壞。隋文帝楊堅統一全國後休養生息，但煬帝楊廣即位後連年用兵：610年征吐谷渾，612至614年三征高句麗，每次都動用百萬之眾，轉輸之費更倍於戰費。丁口大量死於兵役與飢疫，租調與力役年年加派，鄉里青壯多被抽離本業，留在鄉間的老弱與逃亡戶另成一股力量。天災與歉收接連而至，江淮與河南一帶的饑荒最為嚴重；地方倉庫空虛，饑民聚為「盜」，州郡武力不足以彈壓，而朝廷遠在江都，詔令數月才到州縣。及至李淵五月在長安起兵、竇建德與李密在河北河南割據、杜伏威與蕭銳在江南爭雄，隋朝在地方的號令力已近乎名存實亡。益州一地的直接導因則更近：蜀郡是隋在南方的儲糧與轉運重地，役使與加派同樣沉重；州縣之吏多出本地豪族，郡兵與縣兵的組成又以鄉里為主，朝廷對蜀中的掌控倚賴吏與兵的自效，這在秩序動搖時最易崩解。李軌正是看清了這一點，才敢在沒有外援、沒有器械的情況下先發制人。至於起事是否有公開的政治綱領或成文的號令，史料並無記載；可以確定的是，起事打在蜀中政權最薄弱的時節與地點，起事者所要的，是對郡縣控制權與本地秩序的重新瓜分。
causeEn: Li Gui's rising in the winter of Daye 13 (617) had its roots in the general breakdown of the Sui state machinery. Emperor Wen of Sui, Yang Jian, had rested the country after the unification, but once Yang Guang, the Jian emperor, took the throne the wars came without end: the campaign against the Tuyuhun in 610, and the three campaigns against Goguryeo between 612 and 614, each of them committing hundreds of thousands of men, with the cost of moving them and their supplies exceeding the cost of the fighting itself. Huge numbers died in the levies and in famine and epidemic; the land tax and the corvée were increased year by year; the young men of the villages were drawn away from their trades, and the old, the weak and the runaways left behind formed a force of their own. Disasters and poor harvests followed one another, and the famine was worst in the lower Yangtze and in Henan. The local granaries were emptied, hungry men gathered into bands of 'bandits', the armed strength of the commanderies was not enough to contain them, and the court sat at Jiangdu so that an edict took months to reach a county. By the time Li Yuan rose at Chang'an in May, while Dou Jiande and Li Mi held great positions in Hebei and Henan and Du Fuwei and Xiao Rui fought over Jiangnan, the Sui's power to command the provinces was little more than a name. The immediate cause in Yizhou was closer at hand: Shu was one of the Sui's southern storehouse and transport centres, and the burden of labour and extra levies weighed on it just as heavily. The functionaries of the commanderies and counties were largely drawn from the local wealthy families, and the commandery and county troops were themselves recruited from the villages, so that the court's hold on Shu rested on the self-discipline of its clerks and soldiers - the first thing to fail once order shook. Li Gui saw exactly this, and dared to strike first without outside help and without siege equipment. As for whether the rising had a published political programme or a written manifesto, the records say nothing; what can be stated is that it fell at the moment and the place where the Shu authorities were weakest, and what its authors wanted was a new division of control over the commanderies and the local order of the country.
impact: 這場起事本身的直接戰果有限，卻是隋在益州權威終結的標記，也為唐朝接掌西南做了鋪墊。隋朝在蜀中的統治原本靠三樣東西維持：郡縣的官吏、倉庫的儲糧，以及由成都直達長安的蜀道傳遞。起事一發，官府一度退守城邑，糧場與漕運中斷，成都平原的秩序交給了自相擁立的部帥；雖然起義軍在數月內即被平定，但它證明益州已非朝廷可以單憑詔令與一紙文書控制的邊地，唐廷接手時必須用軍事手段重新建立權威。對後世而言，第一重影響是行政上的：唐在益州設大都督府，遣長史總領軍政，把原本分散於州郡的兵、財、糧統一編入幕府體系，蜀地從此成為唐朝西南的軍政基地，其後唐軍經略西南、平定吐蕃與南詔的諸役，多以成都為屯糧與出兵的支點，劍南一線的開發亦自此加速。第二重影響是地方社會的：起事中倒向起義軍的鄉里首領多有兵自重、糧在手，起義雖平，這些人並未全數被清除，多被唐廷收編為郡兵、團練或州兵，官府在蜀中的徵發方式因此由驅民為兵轉向募兵與就地鎮守。第三重影響是象徵與記憶：李軌的名字在唐代以前的正史中只留下寥寥數筆，卻成為「隋末吏變、天下崩解」的一個典型樣本；每逢王朝更替、蜀地饑饉或中央羸弱，蜀中就容易出現類似的起事，而成都平原的糧產與水利，始終是這類事件能否壯大的關鍵。
impactEn: The direct military results of this rising were limited, but it marked the end of Sui authority in Yizhou and paved the way for the Tang takeover of the southwest. Sui rule in Shu had rested on three things: the functionaries of the commanderies and counties, the grain stored in the granaries, and the post road that carried messages from Chengdu straight to Chang'an. When the rising began the officials fell back behind their walls, the granaries and the river transport were broken, and the order of the Chengdu plain passed to band leaders who had proclaimed themselves; although the insurgents were put down within a few months, they had shown that Yizhou was no longer a province the court could hold with edicts and paper alone, and the Tang had to re-establish its authority there by military means. For later ages the first effect was administrative: the Tang set up a great commandery headquarters at Yizhou and sent a chief administrator to direct military and civil affairs, drawing the troops, money and grain that had been scattered among the commanderies and counties into a single command structure. Shu thereby became the military base for the Tang in the southwest, and later Tang campaigns in the southwest and the campaigns that subdued Tufan and Nanzhao drew their stored grain and their troops from Chengdu; the development of the Jiannan line quickened accordingly. The second effect was on local society. The village leaders who had gone over to the insurgents had arms of their own and grain in their hands, and although the rising was crushed they were not all removed; many were taken into Tang service as commandery soldiers, militia units or provincial troops, so that the way the government raised men in Shu turned from compelling the people into service towards recruiting and holding the ground locally. The third effect was one of symbol and memory: Li Gui's name occupies only a few lines in the standard histories before the Tang, yet it became a typical specimen of the way official power splintered and the realm came apart at the end of the Sui; whenever a dynasty changed, whenever famine struck Shu or the centre grew weak, risings of the same kind appeared again, and the grain yield and the waterworks of the Chengdu plain remained the deciding factor in whether such a rising could grow.
result: 起事最終失敗。益州先後經歷官軍進剿與唐軍接管兩個階段：起義軍在成都平原攻取城邑、聲勢最盛之後，因缺乏統一編制、糧秣與攻具而無法轉入攻勢，部眾在官軍合圍與據點收復之下逐步潰散；其首領李軌的下場，傳世記載說法不一，或云為部下所誅，或云為官軍擒殺，無論何說，都意味著這場以他為核心的割據在數月之內終結。平亂之後，益州各郡縣重歸官府管轄，被占的城邑復歸官軍控制，受損的橋樑、倉場與城防重新修整，戶籍與賦役按新朝制度重編；依附起義軍的鄉里首領多被收編為州兵、郡兵或團練，地方秩序在唐初的框架下重新建立起來。李軌起事之後，益州一直到唐玄宗天寶年間都未再出現同等規模的兵亂，蜀地反而成為唐朝最穩定、最富足的支撐之一。就全局而言，李軌起事在隋末的諸多變亂中規模有限、壽命短暫，既沒有像李密那樣撼動中原，也沒有像竇建德那樣建立割據政權，但它是益州從隋入唐的關鍵節點：唐朝在蜀中的第一代將領與第一套幕府制度，都因平定這場起事而開始落地。
resultEn: The rising ended in failure. Yizhou passed through two stages, an advance by government troops and then the takeover by the Tang. After the insurgents had taken the towns of the Chengdu plain and reached the height of their strength, the lack of a unified establishment, of supply and of siege equipment prevented them from turning the offensive; their bands dissolved piecemeal as the government closed in and took back one strongpoint after another. The fate of their leader Li Gui is told differently in the records that survive: some say he was killed by his own men, others that he was captured and put to death by the government. On either reading, the separatism built around him ended within a matter of months. After the suppression, the commanderies and counties of Yizhou returned to official administration; the cities that had been occupied came back under government control; damaged bridges, granaries and defences were repaired; the registers and the tax and corvée were rewritten under the new dynasty's rules. The village leaders who had attached themselves to the insurgents were for the most part enrolled as provincial troops, commandery soldiers or militia, and the local order was rebuilt inside the framework of the early Tang. After Li Gui's rising, Yizhou saw no comparable military disturbance until the Tianbao era of Emperor Xuanzong, and Shu instead became one of the steadiest and wealthiest supports of the Tang. In the wider picture, Li Gui's rising was of limited scale and short life among the many upheavals of the late Sui: it did not shake the Central Plain as Li Mi's did, nor did it build a separatist state as Dou Jiande's did, but it was the hinge on which Yizhou passed from Sui to Tang, and the first generation of Tang commanders in Shu and the first set of command institutions there both took root in the work of putting it down.
